title: Raga Tukhari
hookLine: a raga of cold months and deep feeling

cards: Frost on a windshield at six in the morning. Breath you can see. A field gone stiff and white, every blade of grass holding still.

Cold has its own quiet, and it can make a person feel very far from whoever they love. After the drums of Maru, the Guru Granth Sahib turns to a raga this path hears as one of cold months and deep feeling: Tukhari.

teach.h: A BRIDE, WAITING FOR THE BELOVED.
teach.b: Tukhari holds long, flowing songs of the Gurus, and their mood is longing: a soul like a bride waiting for her Beloved, the Creator, and feeling the distance.
To hear that mood at its coldest, go to one verse in Guru Nanak's poem of the months, which opens in full tomorrow. It's the verse for Poh, a winter month.
In plain English, not word for word: in Poh the frost falls, and the sap dries up in the forest and the grass. The bride asks, in effect, why haven't you come? Listen to the picture.
Everything alive pulls its sap inward and goes still. That's the winter feeling of this raga: not loud grief, but a quiet ache, the kind that settles in when someone you love is far away.

One small detail: the word in that verse for frost is tukhar, very close to the raga's own name. Whether or not the two are related, they keep each other company on the page. And notice what the verse does with the cold.
It doesn't pretend it's warm. It names the frost and the dryness, then turns the whole feeling toward the One it longs for. In this poem, longing isn't a failure of faith.

teach.h: LONGING IS A FORM OF LOVE.
teach.b: It's a form of love. A raga that sings winter honestly takes missing someone seriously.

how: Shabads from the Tukhari section, including Guru Nanak's poem of the months, are sung in Raga Tukhari in kirtan.

games.q: what's inside the raga — tap the pairs.

s: in the Granth, longing for God is a sign of weak faith
Tukhari treats longing as a form of love, and sings it honestly.
Guru Nanak's verse for Poh pictures frost and sap drying up
in Poh the frost falls, and the sap dries in the forest and the grass.
Tukhari's winter mood is loud grief
it's quiet: frost, stillness, an ache for someone far away.

games.q: you're the bride in the Poh verse. the frost has fallen and your Beloved hasn't come. what does the verse do with the cold?
o: names the frost and turns the longing toward the Beloved.
games.why: the verse names the frost and the dryness, then asks, in effect, why haven't you come? the longing itself is turned toward the One.

practice: Let your shoulders drop and your hands rest, the way a winter field goes quiet, and bring to mind someone you miss, far away or gone; don't push the feeling away or stir it up, just let it be present the way frost is on the grass.
If you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe out, turning the missing toward the One; if you don't, simply hold that person in mind with care.
If missing someone ever grows heavier than you can carry, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
